Books, lecture notes, technical texts, and other long-form academic materials
developed throughout my teaching, research, and professional activities.

This section is intended not only as a publication list, but also as a
long-term repository for educational and technical material that may remain
useful beyond the context in which it was originally produced.

## Books

This section will contain published books and substantial monographs.

For each work, whenever available, the archive will provide bibliographic
information together with links to the publisher, DOI, ISBN, electronic
version, source files, or preserved copies.

## Lecture Notes & Textbooks

Teaching materials developed for undergraduate and graduate courses form an
important part of this collection.

Topics include:

- mathematical foundations for computer science;
- information security;
- cryptography;
- digital signatures;
- public key infrastructure;
- digital identity;
- electronic documents;
- blockchain and cryptocurrencies;
- artificial intelligence and security;
- security and usability in information systems.

Some of these materials originated as course notes and evolved over several
years of teaching. Where appropriate, they will be reorganized and preserved
as independent academic texts.

## Technical Texts

This collection will also include substantial technical material produced
outside the conventional scientific-publication workflow.

Examples include:

- technical reports;
- technology studies;
- architecture documents;
- security analyses;
- cryptographic infrastructure studies;
- standards-related material;
- implementation guides;
- institutional technical documents.

When possible, public versions will be preserved together with their original
publication context and associated projects.

## Works in Progress

Some texts are being developed as living documents and may evolve into books,
tutorials, technical reports, or educational resources.

This section will provide access to public versions of these works when they
reach an appropriate stage of development.

## Preservation and Versions

Long-form academic material frequently exists in several forms: drafts,
course editions, institutional reports, preprints, published versions, and
revised editions.

The archive will therefore distinguish between a **work** and its individual
**versions**.

Whenever appropriate, preserved works may include:

- bibliographic metadata;
- publication date;
- version history;
- PDF;
- source files;
- DOI or other persistent identifier;
- associated software or datasets;
- related publications;
- related courses;
- related projects.

The objective is to preserve both the intellectual work and enough context
to understand its evolution.
